1 · What to fix

Over 2537 ms the CPU was busy 41% and 25 outbound network calls took 395 ms combined.

Of the 789 ms render: load functions 19.4 ms + 369 ms waiting · other 270 ms · component render 62.1 ms · remote functions 0.00 ms + 39.5 ms waiting.

3 calls ran one after another for 111 ms: GET 127.0.0.1:4181/hell/api/pricing, GET 127.0.0.1:4181/hell/api/inventory, timer · rows (routes/hell/+page.server.ts:13). Started together they would cost 59.8 ms — about 51.6 ms saved. → Start them together (Promise.all) when they are independent; a call that needs an earlier result stays sequential.

16 calls to 127.0.0.1:4181/hell/api/product/:id — one per item, 112 ms together. → Batch them: one request with the ids (or a bulk endpoint), or fetch the list with its children included.

Biggest CPU consumer: @ionic/core (415 ms, 40.8% of busy time).

Most expensive component: Root at 191 ms total. show the row ↓

ds.render ran 242 times in one render (lib/hell/ds-ssr.ts:46), together: 175 ms of wall for 22478 ms of summed work, 92.1 ms each. Most of it is tag ion-chip: 96 of them, 175 ms of wall (8148 ms summed). → They already overlap, so batching gains little: the cost is each one (make it cheaper, or cache it) and how many there are (render fewer).

ds.pass took 245 ms of the render (ds_ssr (lib/hell/ds-ssr.ts:225)). → The profiler cannot see inside it — this is the wait to take to whoever owns that service, or to cache.

ds.render.all took 176 ms of the render (processDsTags (lib/hell/ds-ssr.ts:38)). → The profiler cannot see inside it — this is the wait to take to whoever owns that service, or to cache.

stock.lookup ran 16 times in one render (load (routes/hell/+page.server.ts:79)), 114 ms together, 7.05 ms each. Most of it is key P0: 1 of them, 7.53 ms of wall. → Once per item is the N+1 shape: batch it (one call for all the ids), or fetch the parent with its children included.

ogygia added 11.1 ms to the render: 52 islands, seed 255 KB, props 126 KB, remote seed 164 B.

The page seed is 255 KB: an island reads $page, so that much of page.data ships to the browser and is serialized on every render. → Read only the keys the island needs (page.data.x, not page.data) so seed shaping trims it, or pass the values as props.

PriceTicker, ProductCard read page.data whole, so every key ships in the seed (255 KB, the biggest is catalog at 225 KB). → Read the keys by name (page.data.catalog, not a spread or a loop over page.data) so seed shaping can drop the rest, or pass the values in as props.

The seed (255 KB) left the JSON lane because of catalog.facets (Map) — devalue writes and revives it several times slower than JSON.parse. → Send that value as a plain string or number (a Date as toISOString(), a Map as an object), or keep it out of page.data.

MegaHeader's props (111 KB) use devalue because of config.updated (Date). → JSON props parse on the fast lane in the browser: pass the value as a string or number, or derive it inside the island.

ProductCard has 48 copies on the page, each waking on visible with its own 80 B of props. → One island around the list hydrates once; or wake: 'interaction' so a copy pays only when touched.

routes/hell/+page.server.ts started only after routes/hell/+layout.server.ts finished (65.8 ms later) — Kit runs a page load and its layout loads together unless the page awaits parent(). → Move the await parent() below the page's own fetches (start them first, await parent() after), or pass what the page needs some other way — the two loads then overlap.

routes/hell/+layout.ts is a universal load: on this render it waited 24.9 ms on calls. On a page with the client router it runs again in the browser on every navigation, and its data must be serializable. → If it only needs the server (a database, a secret, a private API), rename it +layout.server.ts and the browser never runs it.

ProductCard (island host) renders 48 ProductCard rows per render, 43.7 ms together (0.91 ms each). → The list is the cost, not the row: page it, window it, or defer the part below the fold into a hole. show the row ↓

GET 127.0.0.1:4181/hell/api/session waited 45.6 ms; its own Server-Timing says SvelteKit render 45.4 ms, postgres 31.0 ms, render 9.00 ms — 85.4 ms of the wait is on their side, 0.00 ms is the network and their framework. → The wait is theirs: take the biggest entry to whoever owns that service, or cache the response.

The render called its own server 13 times (/hell/api/session, /hell/api/pricing, /hell/api/inventory, …), 293 ms of requests answered by the same event loop that was rendering: the page waited on itself, and every one of those calls paid a full HTTP round trip to reach code in the same process. → Call the function behind the endpoint directly from the load (import it), or use a remote function; keep fetch for servers that are not this one.

The event loop stalled up to 253 ms (p99) — long synchronous work blocks every other request.

Memory grew 144 MB during the window.

The instance was not alone (40 requests ran here during the profiled renders: 40 the page's own calls to itself)

One Node process, one event loop: every other request's turn on the CPU is a wait inside the render's wall time with no frame of its own. Something else was in flight for 37% of the window, taking up to 75.8 ms of CPU from it (an upper bound — a request's CPU is a process-wide delta, so overlapping requests carry some of each other's). None of them is a stranger: they are the page's own calls to this same server, and its holes — the render waited on itself. The CPU tables above exclude the others; the wall time does not.

and 9 more pauses.

A minor pause happens when the young space fills; a major one when the old space grows. Who allocated comes from one read of the allocation profile at the end of the window (reading it during the work set off collections of its own), so "GC ms caused" gives each allocator its share of the pauses by its share of everything allocated, and a pause's "allocated before" is the window's rate over the stretch since the previous pause. "Running then" is what the CPU was doing when the pause fell, from the timeline. The profiler's own allocations are taken out of every pause.

5 · The data

Who reads what (every page.data key: the load that made it, the components that read it, from their sources)

A key read by an island must ship in the seed. A key read only on the server is rendered into the HTML and need not ship. A key nobody reads was fetched for no one — the load's wait behind it is pure waste. The readers come from scanning the route's page and layouts and every component the profile saw; the islands' reads are what the page's own seed explainer recorded, so the two agree. An island that reads the page whole makes every key "unknown".

The data river (upstream calls → loads → page.data keys → the islands that read them)

No island names the keys it reads, so every key ships to every island. Read page.data keys directly in the island (or pass them as props) and the seed shrinks to what is used.

Left to right: what each upstream call cost the load that made it, what each load put into page.data, how big each key is in the seed the browser downloads, and which island reads it. A load whose source the profiler could not read shows its keys as unknown; a key in red ships to no island.

The waits the profiler cannot see on its own, named in the code. Per render: count and time are divided by the 3 renders in this recording. A span appears on the timeline as "in <name>" wherever a call or a gap sits inside it. total is the spans' summed duration, self is that minus the child spans inside them, wall counts overlaps once (∥ marks spans that ran together): wall is what the render paid. A span that carries an attribute with a few distinct values (a tag, a table, a key) gets a by table under it: what each value cost.

Values, not just functions the numbers the spans carried, and how the time moved with them

A span that reports a number (rows, tags, bytes) is measured against it here: ms per unit is the slope of a straight line through the spans, fit how well the line holds (1 = the value alone sets the time). A steep, well-fitting line says the cost is the size of the input; cut the input and the span follows.
